title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given \(n\ge 1, a\) rational P-matrix \(M\in Q^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in Q^{n}\), outputs rational vectors \(z,w\ge 0\) satisfying \(w=Mz+q\) and \(z^{T}w=0\)?
definitions: A principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) uses the same nonempty index set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\) for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when \(\det  M[S,S]>0\) for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial \(p(N)\) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and \(z^{T}w=\sum_{i} z_{i} w_{i}\). There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
why: Test whether uniqueness and complementary linear structure suffice for polynomial-time exact solution of a central optimization search problem.

importance.reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.

context_blocks.text: Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of \(z_{i}\) and \(w_{i}\) must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

ETH’s 2025 research report identifies general P-matrix LCP as a major unresolved optimization question and relates it to unique-sink orientations. The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.
